title: Year two close: the book in your hands
hookLine: a library you've walked through, from the garden to the shore at breakfast

lines: A GARDEN, A DESERT, A ROOM OF SONGS.
THE LAST DAY OF YEAR TWO.
cards: This year began in a garden, where God walked in the cool of the day. Then a desert crossed by a whole people. A room full of songs, some joyful, some furious.
Prophets shouting in the street. Then Luke and John, all the way to a charcoal fire on a beach at dawn where, in John's telling, the risen Jesus cooked breakfast for his friends.
And lately, a few letters left on the table. Today is the last day of year two: one look back, and one verse to take with you.

teach.b: Year two had seven parts. Genesis: beginnings, a garden, a flood, a family that kept going wrong and kept being carried. Exodus: slaves, a sea, manna, a mountain, a golden calf, and long years in the wilderness.
The Psalms and the wisdom books: prayers for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short and good. The prophets: a burning coal, a potter, dry bones, a sulking prophet, a king on a donkey.
Luke: outsiders, meals and mercy. John: the Word, the signs, the bread and the light and the good shepherd, and that breakfast on the shore.
And three letters of joy, faith and love: Philippians, James and First John, with the elder's two short notes. Now the verse.
Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses gives his last speeches before the people cross into the land without him. The commandment, he says, isn't hidden away.

teach.h: NOT IN HEAVEN, NOT ACROSS THE SEA.
teach.b: It isn't up in heaven, where someone would have to climb and fetch it, or across the sea, for someone to sail out and bring back.
In the King James Bible: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Very nigh.
The Hebrew word is karov: close by, within reach.
Paul later quoted this line in his letter to the Romans: "The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart."

teach.h: THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.
teach.b: Jewish and Christian tradition each read the verse in its own way, but the picture is shared: the word isn't a far-off mountain only experts can climb. It's near enough to say, and to keep.
After a year of reading, the book is in your hands.

how: Some Christians keep a favorite verse close, memorized, written in a Bible's margin or posted at home, and churches sometimes mark the end of a season of reading with a time of looking back and giving thanks.

games.q: you're Moses, giving your last speech before the people cross without you. how do you describe God's word?
o: far off, for experts to fetch.
very near: in your mouth and in your heart.
games.why: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it."

practice: Let the year go past and ask which verse stayed: maybe the Lord is my shepherd, a line from a prophet, no fear in love, or something small nobody else would pick.
Choose the one already near you, not the most well-known, and if you can, write it down by hand. If you pray, give thanks for a year of reading.

wordCard.voice: Karov. Hebrew for near, close by: the word Moses said wasn't far off in heaven or across the sea, but near enough to say, and to keep.

orig.note: Hebrew: near, close by. in Deuteronomy 30:14, the word is very near you.
